sentences.text: From question to publication with aff decks: facial expressions during a television commercial
This workshop follows one advertising question from the first sentence a client says to the last sentence of a written results and discussion section.

You will plan a study of how viewers' faces respond to one television commercial, build it in iMotions Lab 11 point 1, set up the webcam and the light, score each face frame by frame, turn the scores into "present" or "absent," test three hypotheses, and write the result for a journal and for a client.
Every section explains why a step exists before it shows how.
Facial expression analysis starts from a description of the face, not of feelings.
The Facial Action Coding System (F A C S) describes any face as a set of action units, numbered movements of particular facial muscles, such as raising the inner brows.
Affectiva aff decks does this coding automatically from video.

In each frame it finds the face, detects action units, and classifies expressions and emotions: seven emotions (Joy, Anger, Surprise, Fear, Contempt, Sadness, and Disgust), valence (how positive or negative the expression is), and engagement (how expressive the face is).
An emotion score runs from 0 to 100 and states the confidence that the expression was shown.
aff decks analyzes only the respondent camera, the webcam aimed at the viewer's face.
If you did Workshop 2, the Aurora measured where the eyes went; this workshop measures what the face did.
What aff decks does not do is read feelings.
The help center says: "Facial expressions provide you information on what is expressed."

The same feeling can show different faces, and the same face can go with different feelings, depending on the person, the situation, and the culture, and measures of emotion taken from the face, the body, and self report agree only in part.
A detected smile is a fact about the face; whether it means enjoyment is an inference the researcher must defend.
Commercials make a natural first face study because advertisers care about moments: when a viewer smiles, and whether smiles go with liking and sharing.

Joy and surprise during video ads have been linked to whether viewers keep watching, research has asked when an ad should entertain, and facial responses have been related to ad liking and purchase intent and to advertising effectiveness.
The worked example is real material: the lab's own study "Nike Campaign Ad Evaluation" in the iMotions Library on the lab computer.
A simulated data set of 32 viewers, built in the same structure, carries the numbers.
Affectiva aff decks is licensed on both lab license keys, so either computer can record and process faces.
Time needed.
About 4 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (question, design, example, build, collect) in the first, 06 to 10 (methods, numbers, analysis, writing) in the second
Equipment.
The lab webcam or the laptop's front camera, good even light from the front, and a lab computer (the laptop or the desktop)
SoftwareiMotions Lab 11 point 1 with Affectiva aff decks, plus R or Excel for section 08
Data files.
The simulated face study files in the site's data folder (facial expression metrics at three thresholds, survey, session log, analysis.
R, the Excel workbook), plus the Nike Campaign Ad Evaluation study in the lab Library, opened in class
How to use.
Work top to bottom, answer each quick check, then tick the section
You need a lab computer with iMotions Lab 11 point 1, a webcam, and this page.
You do not need Workshops 1 or 2 or any experience with iMotions.

The statistics you need are a mean (an average), a median (the middle value when the values are sorted), a standard deviation (how far a typical value sits from the mean), and the idea that a test asks whether a difference is larger than chance would produce.
Every other term is defined where it first appears, and terms with a dotted underline open a one line definition when you tap them.
The help center links open after you sign in through my dot imotions dot com.
At a lab computer, open iMotions in another window to follow the screens in sections 04, 05, and 07.
Nothing in this workshop records into, deletes, or changes the lab's existing studies; open Nike Campaign Ad Evaluation only to look.
Do not record anyone's face, a classmate's included, before exercise 5, where consent comes first.
The one sentence this workshop keeps repeating Decide which expressions, which moments, and which threshold before you look at the data.

aff decks gives at least 29 scores in every frame in which it finds a face (seven emotions, 20 action units, valence, and engagement, plus others such as Attention and head position), a commercial can be cut into moments in many ways, and the threshold that turns a score into "present" changes the size of every number.
A study that chooses after looking will always find a smile somewhere.

Say what aff decks measures (facial movements and expressions) and what it cannot (what the viewer felt), why the moments of a commercial are worth measuring, and which equipment, software, and files this workshop uses.
From idea to research question
A client rarely arrives with a research question.
A client arrives with a business question, a statement of what the business wants to know or to happen.
Picture a brand manager with a finished 60 second commercial: "Does our commercial make people feel something, and when?"
The sentence does not say who will watch, which feeling, how it will be measured, or against what.
A research question names the problem the study will answer and signals the type of study needed.
A hypothesis is a testable answer to it, written with the specific variables that will be measured.
The iMotions design guide asks for both before any data are collected.
The lab asks every study to pass through one sentence with four slots: who, sees what, measured how, compared against what.

Here it reads: adult viewers (who) watch one commercial on the lab monitor after a quiet Baseline screen (sees what), while the respondent camera records the face for aff decks and a rating afterward asks how much they liked the ad (measured how), and each viewer's face during the commercial is compared with the same viewer's face during the Baseline, and the moments of the commercial with one another (against what).
Notice the honest verb: the camera records a face, not a feeling.
Weak questions fail in predictable ways.
"Do people like our ad?"
asks for an opinion, which is reported, not displayed.
"What emotions does the ad cause?"
has every emotion as an answer and claims a cause and a feeling at once.
"Is the ad emotional?"
can be answered yes or no.

The repair names an observable, a measure, and a comparison: "Among the same viewers, is Joy, as aff decks detects it, present for a larger share of the commercial than of the Baseline, and in which 10 second moments is it concentrated?"

In the iMotions table below, the first good question is about a TV ad, but "experiencing positive emotions" is exactly what a camera cannot see; for a face study, read it as "showing positive expressions."
Be exact about what a face study can answer.
Presence: was an expression, a configuration of facial movements such as a smile, detected in a frame or an interval?
Timing: at which moment of the commercial did it appear?
Association: do viewers who show more of an expression also report liking the ad more, or act differently afterward?
It cannot answer what the viewer felt.
An emotion is a state of the person, a feeling with its thoughts and bodily changes; an expression is something the face did.

The iMotions Cognitive Principles Guide says facial expressions "are not necessarily a reflection of a person's internal thoughts or feelings," and the aff decks signal descriptions are themselves careful: a smile is "Normally a sign of enjoyment," and a brow furrow "Can indicate concentration, confusion or dislike."
A viewer can smile out of politeness and can enjoy a commercial with a still face.
Reading a feeling straight off a signal is called reverse inference, and reviews of consumer neuroscience warn against it.
Two traditions supply the vocabulary.
The circumplex model describes affect with two dimensions: valence, how pleasant or unpleasant a state is, and arousal, how calm or activated it is.

aff decks reports valence from the face, but the help center names arousal, the intensity of an emotion, as what facial expression analysis cannot assess: a high smile score is high confidence that a smile is present, a probability that correlates with intensity "but they are not the same."
Its circumplex example takes arousal from skin conductance, the subject of Workshop 4.
The second tradition is the theory of basic emotions: a small set of emotions, each with its own distinctive and universal facial signal.
aff decks's seven emotion scores align, the help center states, with Ekman and Friesen's EMFACS-7, an emotion coding scheme built on F A C S.

A large review found that people do smile when happy more often than chance would predict, but that how they show each emotion varies substantially across cultures, situations, and people, and that one configuration of facial movements can go with more than one emotion (Barrett and colleagues
You need not settle the debate to run a good study, but you must read "Joy" in a data file as the name of a score that responds to a smile.
The hypotheses need three more terms.

F E A thresholding is an iMotions R notebook (a built in analysis routine written in the R language) that turns each 0 to 100 score into present or absent, frame by frame: an expression counts as present when its score passes a threshold, by default 50.
Percent of time present is the share of an interval during which the expression was present.
A binning annotation cuts the commercial into equal intervals, here six bins of 10 seconds, Bin 01 to Bin 06.
Joy is present for more of the commercial than of the Baseline: in the same viewers, Percent of time present for Joy is higher during the commercial.
Joy is not spread evenly across the commercial: Percent of time present for Joy differs across the six 10 seconds bins, and the plan expects it to concentrate in the last two bins, Bin 05 and Bin 06.

Viewers who show more Positive Valence during the commercial like the ad more: Percent of time present for Positive Valence (valence above +50) is positively related to a liking rating from 1 to 7 given after the commercial.
Each hypothesis rests on a reason.
Joy and surprise during video ads have been linked to whether viewers keep watching, and faces recorded by webcam have predicted ad liking (McDuff and colleagues
, 2015), which grounds H1 and H3.
H2 is a timing question: research has asked when an ad should entertain, and the design guide names finding the moments "that connect emotionally" as a goal of video testing.

Advertising research has long set self report, physiological, and facial measures of emotion side by side, including on television ads, which is why H3 pairs a facial measure with a rating instead of letting one stand for the other.
All three tests are two tailed: H1 and H3 state the direction the reasoning predicts, but a result the other way would also matter to the client.
A study run to see what the faces do will find something The iMotions design guide puts it plainly: "Biometric measures are granular enough that you can almost always find some result."

aff decks gives at least 29 scores for every frame in which it finds a face (seven emotions, 20 action units, valence, and engagement, plus others such as Attention, Sentimentality, Confusion, and head position), each summarized in nine intervals at any threshold.

Test only those 29 scores for a commercial against Baseline difference at three thresholds and you have run 87 tests; if no real difference existed anywhere, about one test in twenty, four or so in all, would still come out significant at the point 0 5 level.
The remedy is to choose the expressions, the measure, the moments, and the threshold before the data exist.

Here Joy is the primary expression for H1 and H2 and Positive Valence for H3; the primary measure is Percent of time present at the default threshold of 50; the moments are the six bins; and thresholds of 25 and 75 are named in advance as a sensitivity analysis, a rerun that shows how much a result depends on one choice.
Surprise, Brow Furrow, and Negative Valence are labeled secondary, to be described and not tested.
Filing that plan, dated, before collection is called preregistration, and it lets a reader tell a prediction from a story told afterward.

Turn a client's business question into a research question and a one sentence comparison, say what a face study can answer (presence, timing, association) and what it cannot (the felt emotion), write three hypotheses with one primary measure each, and explain why fishing through the 29 or more aff decks scores finds chance.
Designing a face study around a baseline
A design is the set of decisions that make a comparison fair.
For a face study the first is what each viewer's face during the commercial is compared against, and the answer is the same viewer's face at rest.
Faces differ at rest: one mouth turns up a little, one brow sits low.
Webcams, distance, and light differ between sessions too.
A Baseline, a neutral screen shown before the commercial, records each viewer's resting face under that day's conditions.
Comparing the commercial with it makes the design within subjects: every viewer supplies both conditions, so stable differences between faces, cameras, and rooms drop out of the comparison.
aff decks does part of this on its own.

The help center explains that it "has historically not required a baseline neutral stimulus" because of a rolling baseline: each frame is compared with the faces the same person makes in past and future frames, which subtracts a persistent resting face.

So the Baseline here is not a calibration of aff decks but a comparison period, as in the iMotions demonstration study of video commercials: "it is often useful to add a 'baseline' to the study to compare your results against."
If you did Workshop 2, its order was balanced; here the Baseline always comes first, so the commercial minus Baseline difference also contains settling into the chair, a cost to report.
The real study and the simulated data share this structure, and each part has a job.
In the plan, an instruction slide first gives every viewer the same words: "Watch the screen as you would at home; you do not need to do anything."
It must not name the brand or say that the study is about emotion, because a viewer who guesses what the researcher hopes to see tends to supply it, a demand effect.
The design guide's video ad example adds: "Please do not obstruct your face during the session and keep your hands relaxed."
An average over 60 seconds can hide a strong response that lasted five, so the plan fixes, before collection, how the commercial will be cut into moments.
A stimulus annotation marks an interval of a stimulus once for every respondent; the help center recommends stimulus annotations for video commercials.

A binning annotation cuts a stimulus into intervals of equal length; the iMotions commercial demo suggests "a 'binning' annotation with a fixed duration (for example, of 5 seconds)," or annotations that mark scenes such as the end scene.
This plan uses six 10 second bins, Bin 01 (0 to 10 seconds) to Bin 06 (50 to 60 seconds).
Scene annotations drawn from the storyboard, the shot by shot plan of the commercial, carry more meaning.
Either works if it is fixed before anyone is recorded, because bin edges chosen after seeing the smiles let the data draw their own boundaries.

The design guide also warns that "it typically does not make sense to use facial expression analysis when testing static images," and even during a good commercial spontaneous expressions are small and rare: expect many viewers to show no Joy at all during a quiet Baseline, and plan for those zeros (section 03).
Consent is stricter here than in any other workshop.
A face video, the respondent camera recording, identifies the viewer outright and is the most sensitive file the lab keeps.
iMotions guidance treats face recordings as personal data, and each export of respondent camera recordings writes a separate video file for every stimulus and respondent.

Informed consent is a documented explanation, given before participation, of the purpose, that taking part is voluntary and can be withdrawn, the participant's rights, how the data will be handled, and the risks.

For face video the handling part must match what the lab actually stores: that the face is recorded on video and scored by software; who may watch the video; where it is stored; when it is deleted; whether any image of the face will appear in a report; and that a viewer who withdraws can have it deleted.
Post processing (section 07) works from the video itself, so the video is kept at least until processing is final, and the form must say so.
A form that promises anonymity while a face video sits on the laptop is false.
Privacy concerns raised for gaze data apply even more to faces, and the N M S B A code of ethics sets out participants' rights (Neuromarketing Science and Business Association, n.d.)
At Jacksonville State a study that will be published or presented first goes to the Institutional Review Board (I R B), the committee that reviews research with human participants.
The main comparison is paired: each viewer's commercial against the same viewer's Baseline.
The paired t test works on each viewer's difference, so the stable part of each viewer cancels.
The effect size for paired data is d z, the mean of the differences divided by their standard deviation.
Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it is real; the usual target is 80 percent.
In plain words.

For a large effect, d z equals 0.8, a paired test at two tailed alpha point 0 5 and 80 percent power needs 15 usable viewers; a medium effect, d z equals 0.5, needs 34; a small one, d z equals 0.3, needs 90, the same numbers as in Workshop 2.
The same calculation in G*Power G*Power, Means: difference between two dependent means (matched pairs), two tails, d z equals 0.5, alpha point 0 5, power 80 percent: total sample size 34.
G*Power is the program most researchers cite for this.
Cohen's small, medium, and large conventions were written for differences between groups, so they only roughly guide d z.
With many zeros in face data, the primary test will be rank based (section 08), so treat this as a benchmark.

Face studies lose viewers in their own ways: glare on glasses lenses hides the eyes and brows, a viewer who looks down leaves the picture ("The face must be fully in view for the algorithm to detect the face"), and uneven light washes the face out.
Plan to lose one viewer in five to one in four (20 to 25 percent), and schedule by one rule: the usable viewers needed divided by the share you expect to keep (1 minus the expected loss), rounded up.
For d z equals 0.5, 34 divided by 0.80 equals 42.5, so 43, and 34 divided by 0.75 equals 45.3, so 46: schedule about 43 to 46, within the design guide's 20 to 60 people per study condition.
Adding 20 percent to 34 is not the same: 41 viewers, less one in five, leaves 32.8, short of 34.
Then write the exclusion rule.

After post processing, iMotions reports for each recording a quality value, here called Data quality, that is "only representative of the percentage of frames successfully analyzed," a measure of face detection and not of accuracy.

The manuals state no minimum, so the lab sets its own rule in advance: a viewer whose Data quality is below 80 percent is excluded, and the session log records glasses, lighting, and anything that took the face out of view.
A rule chosen after seeing who looks bad is chosen to get a result.
Last, one commercial is one stimulus, a specific thing shown to viewers, not a sample of commercials.
Whatever the faces did belongs to everything in it at once: story, music, people on screen, product, brand.
The result can say that this commercial, as made, went with more Joy than the Baseline in these viewers.
It cannot say that humor or emotional advertising in general produces smiles; that needs many commercials analyzed as a sample, called stimulus sampling.

Explain why each viewer is compared with his or her own Baseline, give each part of the session a job, fix the bins and the exclusion rule in advance, write consent that matches the face video you keep, plan the sample with d z and a margin for lost faces, and say what one commercial can show.
The worked example in full
Sections 01 and 02 fit on one page, the first deliverable of any study in this lab.
Below is the commercial study as a student plan; change the commercial, the bins, and the numbers, and it becomes your own.

Is Joy, as aff decks detects it, present for more of a 60 seconds commercial than of a neutral Baseline, in which 10 seconds moments is it concentrated, and do viewers who show more Positive Valence like the ad more?
H1: Percent of time present for Joy is higher in the commercial than in the Baseline.

H2: Joy is not spread evenly across the commercial: Percent of time present for Joy differs across the six 10 seconds bins, and the plan expects it to concentrate in the last two bins, Bin 05 and Bin 06.
H3: Percent of time present for Positive Valence in the commercial is positively related to liking of the ad.
All two tailed.
Within subjects against a baseline: every viewer sees the same fixed sequence once.
Instructions, Baseline (60 seconds, neutral), Commercial (60 seconds), Recovery (15 seconds, neutral), then a questionnaire (liking, brand attitude, sharing).
"Watch the screen as you would at home; you do not need to do anything," in the same words for every viewer, with the request not to cover the face.
One binning annotation: six 10 seconds bins, Bin 01 (0 to 10 seconds) to Bin 06 (50 to 60 seconds), fixed before collection.
Joy (H1, H2) and Positive Valence (H3).
Surprise, Brow Furrow, and Negative Valence as secondary expressions.
Engagement as a mean raw score from 0 to 100, not thresholded.

F E A thresholding at the defaults, Emotion 50 and Valence +50 (Positive Valence) and -50 (Negative Valence); the help center calls 50 percent confidence "a moderately strong display of facial response."
Sensitivity analysis at 25 and 75.
32 viewers scheduled (V 01 to V 32) for a target of 30 usable, inside the design guide's 20 to 60 per condition.

That is fewer than the plan rule of section 02 would schedule (30 divided by 0.80 equals 37.5, so 38, for a loss of one in five); the simulation lost 2 of 32, about 6 percent, but a real study should schedule by the rule.
For each viewer, interval (Baseline, Commercial, Recovery, each bin), and expression: Percent of time present and the Number of segments, how many separate times the expression passed the threshold.
Across viewers: how many showed the expression at all.
Survey: Ad liking 1to7.
Recording: Data quality ( percent), the percentage of frames aff decks analyzed.
Exclude a viewer whose Data quality is below 80 percent, the lab's own rule; the manuals state no minimum.

H1: a Wilcoxon signed rank test on the Commercial minus Baseline differences (primary), the paired t test and d z beside it, and an exact McNemar test on the viewers with any Joy, all repeated at 25 and 75.

H2: a mixed model with bin as a factor and a random intercept for each viewer, its I C C, two planned contrasts of Bin 05 and Bin 06 against the mean of Bin 01 to Bin 04 with Holm adjustment (set before the data as a check on whether Joy concentrated late in the commercial, in the last two bins, as the plan expects), the Friedman test as a check, and the percent of viewers with Joy per bin.
H3: Pearson and Spearman correlations of Positive Valence time with Ad liking 1to7.
Alpha point 0 5.
A table by interval and bin, three figures, a results section and a discussion in journal form, and a three sentence client summary that says expressions are not feelings.
Section 08 runs these tests; here are the reasons.
Face data are zero inflated: many values are exactly 0, because many viewers never pass the threshold in an interval, so a few expressive viewers pull the mean up.
The Wilcoxon test therefore works on the ranks of the paired differences, and the median, the middle value, sits beside the mean.
McNemar compares how many of the same viewers showed any Joy in each period.

A mixed model is a regression that knows which rows belong to the same viewer; its random intercept gives each viewer an overall level, and the I C C (intraclass correlation) is the share of variation between viewers.

The two contrasts compare each late bin with the mean of the first four because the plan expects Joy in the last two bins; Holm adjustment guards the two contrasts against false positives, Friedman checks the bins on ranks, and Pearson and Spearman correlate values and ranks.
Each hypothesis has one primary measure.

H1 uses Joy Percent of time present, a share rather than seconds, so the Baseline, the commercial, and the bins sit on one scale; the count of viewers with any Joy checks that a higher mean does not come from two or three very expressive faces.
H2 reads the same measure in each bin beside the percent of viewers with Joy, the quantity the optional F E A thresholding Aggregation step displays over time.
H3 uses Positive Valence Percent of time present during the commercial and the liking rating, which no camera can supply.
Everything else is described, not tested.
Surprise, Brow Furrow, and Negative Valence are reported by interval and bin to show what else the faces did.
Engagement differs in kind, for three reasons.
It is not thresholded, so it is a mean raw score per interval rather than a percent of time.
It measures responsiveness "whether positive or negative," so a rise does not say which way the face moved.
And no hypothesis names it: testing it after looking would add an unplanned test, the fishing of section 01.
The real material is "Nike Campaign Ad Evaluation," the lab's own study in the Library on the lab computer.

The lab's operating guide records its structure: a 60 seconds Baseline, a 60 seconds Nike commercial, a 15 seconds Recovery, and a short questionnaire, with the laptop's front camera as the respondent camera for aff decks and a Shimmer3 G S R+ unit for skin conductance.

What the guide does not record (what the commercial shows, how many respondents were recorded, which settings were used, what the questionnaire asks) you find by opening the study on the lab computer, not by guessing.
Wherever a number about viewers appears, it is simulated This workshop reports no results from the Nike study.
Every number about viewers, in any section, comes from a simulated data set built to mirror a study of this kind.
No viewer was recorded for it, and none of its numbers may be quoted as a finding about the Nike commercial or about real viewers.
The simulated files sit in the site's data folder; make simulated data dot P Y (seed 20265798) generated them, and each data file opens with a line that says simulated.
simulated fea metrics dot C S V feeds the statistics: one row per respondent, interval, and expression, so 32 viewers, 9 intervals, and 6 expressions give 1,728 rows.

Its columns are Study Name, Respondent Name (V 01 to V 32), Interval type (Stimulus, or Annotation for the bins), Interval label, Interval duration (s), Expression, Threshold, Percent of time present, Number of segments, Mean raw score (0-100), filled only for Engagement, and Data quality ( percent).

The layout is modeled on the help center's description of the F E A Metrics Export, "how often and how long a facial expression was present for each respondent and each time interval," but the manuals print no real header row, so verify it on the lab machine.
The files ending in threshold25 and threshold75 share the layout.
simulated fea survey dot C S V holds Respondent Name, Gender, Age, Ad liking 1to7, Brand attitude 1to7, and Would share Yes No.

simulated fea session log dot C S V is the operator's log: Respondent Name, Session Date (the dates, October 26 to 29, 2026, are simulated like every other value in the file), Operator, Glasses, Lighting note, Face detection percent (the operator's copy of Data quality), Data complete, and Decision note.
Respondent Name joins the three files.
Two log rows end in exclude: V 07, Data quality 61 percent, with overhead light reflecting on the glasses lenses, and V 19, 72 percent, who looked down at a phone during the commercial.
Both fall below the 80 percent rule, which leaves 30 viewers (all simulated).
The folder also holds analysis dot R, an Excel workbook, and results text dot M D, the model paragraphs that later sections adapt.

One deliverable is a picture over time: an Aggregate Replay graph, the replay view that summarizes all respondents, of how many respondents showed an expression in each time window (verify on the lab machine that it appears for a video stimulus in 11 point 1).
Any such graph must state the expression, the threshold, the window length, and the number of viewers.

Write the one page study plan, pair each hypothesis with its primary measure, explain why Engagement is described and not tested, say what is known about the Nike study without guessing, and say which simulated file answers which question.
From faces to scores: what aff decks measures, what a threshold does, and how to describe it

Every number in a face study ends a chain: the respondent camera records the face, Affectiva aff decks finds it in each video frame and scores its movements, the F E A thresholding notebook turns each score into present or absent, and the export counts how much of each interval an expression filled.
Workshop 2 measured where the eyes went; this workshop measures what the face did.
A methods section names every link, its settings, and the exclusion rule.
The Facial Action Coding System (F A C S) describes any facial movement as action units, numbered muscle movements such as the lip corners pulled up or the brows drawn together.
aff decks automates the coding with computer vision, software that analyzes images, in three steps: face detection, action unit detection, and expression and emotion classification.
"The face must be fully in view," and data exist only "for each frame of video where a face is detected."

The Affectiva (aff decks) Signals Overview groups the output as Behavioral (head Pitch, Yaw, and Roll, that is nodding, turning, and tilting), Facial Expression (action units such as Smile and Brow Furrow), and Emotion (seven core emotions, among them Joy and Surprise, plus Engagement and Valence).

The developer reports an average ROC-AUC (the chance that a frame showing the expression outscores one without it) of 91 percent against "at least 3 F A C S-certified human coders," a vendor figure, not an independent test.
In plain words.
A Joy score of 80 in one frame says the software is fairly confident that the face shows the movement it was trained to call Joy, mainly a smile.
It says nothing about how big the smile is or whether the viewer is happy.
A Joy score of 80 in one frame says the software is fairly confident that the face shows the movement it was trained to call Joy, mainly a smile.
It says nothing about how big the smile is or whether the viewer is happy.

What the manuals sayScores run from 0 to 100, "indicating the confidence that a Facial Expression or Emotion was expressed" (Signals Overview); probability correlates with intensity "but they are not the same" (Introduction to Facial Expression Analysis).
Valence runs from -100 to 100, 0 neutral.

Scores run from 0 to 100, "indicating the confidence that a Facial Expression or Emotion was expressed" (Signals Overview); probability correlates with intensity "but they are not the same" (Introduction to Facial Expression Analysis).
Valence runs from -100 to 100, 0 neutral.
Keep the expression and the emotion apart.
The Signals Overview aligns its emotion scores with EMFACS-7, the emotion version of F A C S, without listing the inputs to Joy; in practice Joy rises with a smile.
Its table calls a smile "Normally a sign of enjoyment" and says a Brow Furrow "Can indicate concentration, confusion or dislike": note normally and can.
The same facial movement can accompany different feelings, and the same feeling can show differently or not at all, across people, situations, and cultures (Barrett and colleagues
, 2019), and measures of emotion agree only in part.
So write "Joy was present," never "viewers felt joy"; the step between them is an inference the researcher must defend.
Valence counts Smile among its inputs, so Positive Valence moves with Joy, and Engagement "measures the level of expressiveness and involvement" (module page), not attention.

An average of confidence scores mixes weak evidence everywhere with strong evidence in a few frames, so the F E A thresholding R Notebook marks an expression present in each frame where its score passes the threshold.
The defaults are Emotion 50, Valence +50 (Positive Valence) and -50 (Negative Valence), and Action Units 50.

"50 percent confidence represents a moderately strong display of facial response," 75 or higher is high confidence, and 25 or lower "means that only 1 in 4 manual coders has classified the facial expression as present."

Explore pilot data, then fix the threshold before testing; it is a measurement decision, like the A O I shape if you did Workshop 2: mean Joy time in the commercial was 17.76 percent at a threshold of 25, 10.37 at 50, and 4.21 at 75 (simulated).
Report it.

The F E A thresholding Metrics give, per respondent and interval (a stimulus, an annotation, or a scene), the percent of stimulus time with the expression present and the number of segments, separate stretches of presence that show "how often it was expressed"; each segment's onset and offset is marked as an event.
The simulated export calls the first Percent of time present and the second Number of segments; the manuals print no header row, so verify both on the lab machine.
Joy present for 6 seconds of the 60 seconds commercial, in two stretches, gives a Percent of time present of 10 and a Number of segments of 2.
The binning annotation cuts the commercial into six 10 seconds bins, so the Commercial value is the mean of the six bin values.
How many viewers showed the expression in a time window is what the F E A thresholding Aggregation draws in the Aggregate Replay.
This course counts a viewer when Percent of time present is above 0; the manual does not state the Aggregation's own rule, so verify it on the lab machine.
After post processing, Quality Metrics report "the percentage of frames successfully analyzed," which is "not an indicator of overall accuracy or face quality."
Live values run lower, because aff decks processes a 30 hertz camera at 15 hertz while recording, so 40 to 50 percent "is not cause for concern" before post processing.

Frames are lost with a bright background, a face darker than 30 on the 0 to 255 brightness scale (the manual states this rule right after a sentence about bright backgrounds, so which failure it describes is an item to verify on the lab machine), a Facebox (the box around the detected face) under 100 px wide, hair, hands, or glasses over the face, talking, or a head turned beyond "5-10 degrees up/down and 40 degrees left/right" (Enabling Affectiva aff decks in iMotions).

Building the study: the respondent camera, aff decks, and the flow
aff decks can score only what the respondent camera recorded, and only if the camera and aff decks were on before the viewer sat down.
So the build has three layers, all settled before the first session: the computer (which camera records the face, and whether aff decks runs), the study (its sensors and screens), and the plan.
If you did Workshop 2, the Study Builder is the same; only the sensor changes.
Either lab computer works, because aff decks is licensed on both keys.
Camera settings live in Global Settings, the dialog for settings that apply to the whole computer rather than to one study.
Open Global Settings.
Press Alt plus G or choose Preferences, then Global Settings; the Preferences menu sits in the menu bar at the upper left, beside File.
You should see a dialog with nine tabs: Eye tracking, Calibration, Slide Show, Stimuli, Results, Audio and Video, Sensors, API, and Packages.
Common mistake.
Choosing Sensor Settings (Alt plus S), just below it, which opens the same dialog on the Sensors tab; click Audio and Video instead.
Choose the camera.
On the Audio and Video tab, under Camera Setup, select Respondent under Select Camera To Configure, tick 'Enable VideoCam Capture', and choose the input in the list beside it.
On the lab computer in October 2026 the input read Integrated Webcam, the laptop's built-in camera; if you plug in an external webcam, choose it instead and write down its model.
You should see your face in the camera preview.
If Windows reports "Access to the camera was denied," set "Allow desktop apps to access your camera" to On in the Windows camera privacy settings.

Configuring the Scene or Environment camera: facial expression analysis is "only available for recordings from the Respondent Camera."
Set the resolution and frame rate.
The resolution, the size of each frame in pixels, sets how many pixels the face gets; the frame rate, the frames recorded per second, sets how many frames aff decks can score.
"Most cameras allow at least 640 by 480 video resolution at 20-30 frames per second," and higher settings add processing and memory load.
The Facebox, the box aff decks draws around a detected face, "should be at least 100px" wide.
On the lab computer one list sets both: it read 1280 by 720 at 30, which means 1280 by 720 pixels at 30 frames per second, with an Options button beside it.
Include Audio was ticked on the lab computer, with the laptop microphone chosen; untick it unless the plan needs sound, because a voice makes a face video easier still to identify.
Below the preview, an Encoding Quality slider and a codec list (H 264) set how the video file is compressed; leave both as you find them.
You should see your choice in the resolution list.

Not writing the camera model, resolution, and frame rate in the study notes; the methods paragraph (section 06) needs all three.

On the same tab, below the camera, find the section titled Affectiva aff decks Video Analysis, tick Enable Data Collection, and click OK.
You should see the box ticked; the Facebox and the aff decks signals then appear in the Sensor Preview (section 05).

Camera, light, and the session
aff decks scores only a face it can find: "The face must be fully in view for the algorithm to detect the face."
Most of what decides that is fixed before anyone clicks Start Recording: where the camera sits, how the light falls, and what the viewer does with hands, hair, glasses, and phone.
There is no calibration, as there was for the Aurora if you did Workshop 2; the check is the live preview.
The camera "should be set at eye level and directed to the front of the respondent's face," placed so that the face stays in the picture when the viewer shifts a little.

On the lab monitor that means a webcam on the bezel of a monitor that tilts toward the viewer; on the laptop, raise the laptop until its front camera is at eye level instead of looking up at the chin.
aff decks 5.1 and newer reads heads turned "ideally between 5-10 degrees up/down and 40 degrees left/right," so the camera belongs on the screen that plays the commercial.
Use a fixed chair without wheels.
Phones go away before the session, and hair, hands, hats, and sunglasses stay clear of the face; talking, gum, and eating spoil the scores.
Ordinary glasses are allowed, but check them for glare.
"Best results are obtained with uniform, diffused illumination of the face against a dark, contrasting background."

Light that falls straight on the face or the monitor obscures expressions, and a bright window or lamp behind the viewer washes the face out; the manual adds that detection is lost when the face's average brightness falls below 30 on a scale from 0 (black) to 255 (white), though which failure that rule describes is an item to verify on the lab machine (section 06).
The iMotions lab recommendations suggest dispersed light from a lamp pointed against the wall behind the respondent, and blackout curtains if the room gets sunlight.
The simulated session log records the fixes the lab uses: overhead lights dimmed, blinds lowered, a lamp against the wall, and the monitor tilted slightly down.
In the simulated data, V 07's glasses reflected the overhead light, the glare hid the eyes and brows for long stretches, and Data quality fell to 61 percent.
The Sensor Preview is the window that shows the live sensor data.
Check it on your own face before the viewer arrives, and on the viewer's face once seated.
Open it.
Click Sensor Preview beside Start Recording (F12 on a two screen setup).

You should see the Respondent Camera panel with two numbers over the video: at the top left the aff decks processing rate over the camera's capture rate ("Typical processing for a standard 30 hertz camera, is 10-20 aff decks frames per second"), and at the top right the Facebox width.
Common mistake.
Judging the picture by eye; a face that looks fine to you may be too dark or too small for aff decks.
Read the face.
Good: the Facebox and the aff decks landmarks sit on the face, the width is at least 100 px, and the face does not fill the frame.
Bad: "No Face Detected!"
with a processing rate of 0 and a width of 0px, which means the position or the focus is wrong (section 06 shows a detected face beside a missing one).
Fix the camera, the light, or the seat before you record.
Watch the signals.
Open the Signals menu, where 'Affectiva aff decks' should be listed with its Behavioral, Emotion, and Facial Expression groups, and click to the left of a signal to show it in the Signals panel.
"Check that the graphs are streaming live and that the data fluctuates as expected": on your own face, smile and frown to see Joy and Brow Furrow move.
With a viewer, check only the Facebox and the numbers; asking a viewer to smile rehearses the very response the study measures, a demand effect.

The help center says the Sensor Data Preview during a recording is "only available when running the experiment on a dual-screen setup," so whether the operator can watch the face while the commercial plays depends on the lab layout; verify on the lab machine.
Before the viewer arrives: the camera and aff decks checked on your own face, the study selected, the log open, and any live markers defined.

A live marker is a time stamp the operator adds with a key during recording, and "You have to define your Live Markers before starting the data recording": on the study's Live Markers tab, type a Name, choose a key combination and a color, and click Add Marker.
Useful operator markers name the problems of a face study, such as "Face covered" or "Talking."
Consent.
Obtain informed consent with the form from section 02, which names the face video, who may watch it, where it is stored, and when it is deleted (Neuromarketing Science and Business Association, n.d.)
Seat and check.
Seat the viewer, adjust the camera and the light, and confirm the Facebox in the preview.
Record.
Select or add the respondent with the anonymous I D from the log (V 01, V 02, and so on) and click Start Recording.
iMotions warns at the start if the study and Global Settings disagree; stop and fix the setting instead of clicking past it.
Common mistake.
Recording a respondent a second time, which overwrites the data.
Let it run.
The Instructions, Baseline, commercial, Recovery, and questionnaire run on their own.
Sit out of the viewer's sight and stay silent.
If something happens, press a live marker key where the preview allows it and note the time.
End Recording (Shift-F1) is only for stopping early; an aborted recording is still saved.
Debrief the viewer and answer questions.
Log.
Write the row in the session log, the operator's record of each session, before the next viewer sits down.
The simulated log has Respondent Name, Session Date, Operator, Glasses, Lighting note, Face detection percent (filled in after post processing), Data complete, and Decision note.
Common mistake.
Excluding a viewer on the spot.
V 19 looked down at a phone during the commercial; the log says so, the recording ran in full, and the 80 percent rule decided after post processing (72 percent, excluded).

After the last stimulus iMotions opens the Recorded Data screen, where each recording shows a quality box per sensor, and "A red outline indicates that the recorded data is below the expected quality for a given sensor."

For aff decks that is normal: "if using the aff decks engine, ALL sessions will show sub-standard data quality at first," because aff decks "renders at 15 hertz during live collection and must be post-processed up to 30 hertz after recording."
Before post processing, a value of 40 to 50 percent "is not cause for concern."

Watch the recording for real problems instead (turning away, a missing face), "especially if the data quality is less than 40 percent": select the study, the respondent, the 'Recorded data' page, and 'Play'.
Privacy concerns raised for gaze data apply even more to a face video, so only the people the consent form names may watch it.

Post processing runs aff decks again on the saved face video.

The replay article warns that "maximally 50 percent of the video frames were analyzed live," and the thresholding article recommends "post processing all respondent videos before starting an analysis of the facial expression data."
Open the dialog.
Right-click the study in the Library and choose Post Processing, then Affectiva; the submenu lists other processors too.
You should see "Affectiva aff decks Processing."

In 11 point 1 the study's Recorded Data tab also shows an Affectiva heading with a Post Process button, beside Exposure summaries and its Calculate button; the menu route is the one the manual documents.
Common mistake.
Choosing Find and blur faces, a different job.
Choose what to process.
Leave "Ignore previous aff decks processed data" unticked the first time; tick it only to redo processing after a fix.
The manuals do not describe "Increase speed through parallel processing of respondent videos per stimulus," so leave it as you find it and verify on the lab machine what it changes.
The help article's slider (n equals 1) and its OK button are not in the 11 point 1 dialog.
Tick Select all under "Select respondents to process:" and under "Select stimuli to process:".
You should see "Process N videos," with N equal to respondents times stimuli.

In the lab's remote study, and in the demonstration study in the figure below, the stimulus Select all box was unticked when the dialog opened (in the remote study the calibration stimuli were left out), so the button read "Process 700 videos" until ticking it gave "Process 924 videos"; the help center requires all stimuli for remote study data.

Processing only the commercial, which leaves the Baseline with live data alone.
Process and wait.
A "Background Jobs" window opens (tabs Job Queue, Completed, and Job Errors), one "Affdex batch" job per respondent, and the status bar counts the jobs beside the Background Jobs button.
Each video takes "roughly the same as the duration of that video," so run a study overnight; closing the window does not stop the jobs.
You should see every job under Completed and none under Job Errors.

Clicking Stop All Jobs to close the window.
Apply the exclusion rule.
Each recording now shows a quality value, "only representative of the percentage of frames successfully analyzed," not of accuracy.

Export the values with Export on the study's Recorded Data tab (a DataQuality dot T X T file with the effective sampling rate and the percentage of data obtained; verify on the lab machine how its rows and its aff decks column are laid out, and say in the plan which value counts), copy them into the log's Face detection percent, and apply the 80 percent rule before anyone looks at an expression: V 07 (61.0) and V 19 (72.0) go and V 20 (87.8) stays (simulated).

Name it by its settings (for example Kept30 Threshold50) and leave the excluded viewers out in the segmentation steps (verify how on the lab machine), so that every count of viewers counts kept viewers.

Keep the default thresholds: Emotion 50, Valence +50 and -50, Action Units 50.
Verify on the lab machine the batch and per channel threshold fields, which the screenshot shows collapsed.

Changing a threshold after seeing the data.
Add the aggregation flow.
Click "+" again for "F E A thresholding Aggregation," the optional step that draws the aggregation graphs and "only works if you have also added the 'F E A thresholding' algorithm in this analysis."

Set Time bin length in milliseconds and Time bin overlap in milliseconds (the screenshot shows 500 and 0; no default is stated, so write yours into the plan) and tick "Display each aggregated curve as a percentage of the total number of respondents."
Choose the stimuli (Baseline, commercial, Recovery) on SELECT STIMULI and complete the analysis.
